The diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis has been extensively studied, with significant contributions from the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2010, which provided detailed insights into diagnostic methodologies. 2. Vassal et al. conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of the Xpert MTB/RIF assay for rapid tuberculosis diagnosis in high-burden countries, highlighting its potential to improve diagnostic efficiency. 3. Kruk, Gie, Schaaf, and Marais explored symptom-based screening for child tuberculosis contacts, emphasizing its feasibility in resource-constrained settings. 4. Keown and colleagues reviewed evidence on medical care screening, providing a comprehensive analysis of its effectiveness. 5. Holland and Stewart examined the role of screening in disease prevention, identifying strategies that yield the most significant benefits. 6. Kranzer et al. systematically reviewed the benefits of active tuberculosis screening for both communities and individuals, emphasizing its importance in public health. 7. Murray and Salomon modeled the global impact of tuberculosis control strategies, offering projections on their potential outcomes. 8. Borgdorff, Floyd, and Broekmans analyzed interventions aimed at reducing tuberculosis mortality and transmission in lowand middle-income countries. 9. Dodd, White, and Corbett investigated the timing of periodic active case finding for tuberculosis, providing guidance on optimal implementation. 10. Dowdy et al. studied the heterogeneity in tuberculosis transmission and the role of geographic hotspots in sustaining epidemics. 11. Legrand et al. modeled the impact of tuberculosis control strategies in overcrowded, high-endemic prisons, offering insights into targeted interventions. 12. Tiemersma et al. conducted a systematic review on the natural history of untreated pulmonary tuberculosis in HIV-negative patients, focusing on disease duration and fatality. 13. Straetemans et al. performed a meta-analysis to assess tuberculosis case fatality ratios, providing a quantitative synthesis of available data. 14. Waitt and Squire systematically reviewed risk factors for mortality during and after tuberculosis treatment in adults. 15. Miller et al. evaluated the personal and societal health quality losses attributable to tuberculosis, emphasizing its broader impact. 16. Rieder provided an epidemiological basis for tuberculosis control, offering foundational knowledge for public health strategies. 17. Frieden edited the second edition of Toman’s Tuberculosis, a comprehensive resource on tuberculosis management published by the World Health Organization. 18. Mitchell et al. assessed the acceptability of tuberculosis screening among at-risk and vulnerable groups, synthesizing qualitative and quantitative findings. 19. Hopewell et al. established international standards for tuberculosis care, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 20. The World Health Organization provided guidance for national tuberculosis programs on managing tuberculosis in children, emphasizing tailored approaches. 21. WHO also issued guidelines on nutritional care and support for tuberculosis patients, recognizing the role of nutrition in disease management. 22. The rapid implementation of the Xpert MTB/RIF diagnostic test was detailed in a WHO report, offering practical considerations for its deployment. 23. WHO policy on collaborative TB/HIV activities provided guidelines for national programs and stakeholders to address co-infection challenges. 24. WHO also released a policy on tuberculosis infection control in healthcare facilities, congregate settings, and households, emphasizing preventive measures. 25. Lönnroth et al. identified a dose-response relationship between body mass index and tuberculosis incidence, highlighting the role of nutrition in disease risk. 26. Cegielski and McMurray reviewed the relationship between malnutrition and tuberculosis, drawing evidence from human and animal studies. 27. Targeted tuberculin testing and treatment of latent tuberculosis infection were recommended in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. 28. Jeon and Murray systematically reviewed the increased risk of active tuberculosis in individuals with diabetes mellitus. 29. Lönnroth et al. examined alcohol use as a risk factor for tuberculosis in a systematic review. 30. Rehm et al. explored the association between alcohol use, alcohol use disorders, and tuberculosis in a systematic review. 31. Lin, Ezzati, and Murray conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the impact of tobacco smoke and indoor air pollution on tuberculosis. 32. Slama et al. reviewed the relationship between tobacco use and tuberculosis, providing a qualitative and meta-analytic perspective. 33. Verver, Warren, and Beyers found that the rate of reinfection tuberculosis after successful treatment is higher than the rate of new tuberculosis cases. 34. Crampin et al. studied recurrent tuberculosis in a general population cohort in Malawi, distinguishing between relapse and reinfection, particularly in the context of HIV. 35. Marx et al. investigated the rate of sputum smear-positive tuberculosis after treatment default in high-burden settings through a retrospective cohort study. 36. Getahun et al. reviewed evidence on the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of tuberculosis in children and mothers, emphasizing maternal and child health services. 37. Figueroa-Damian and Arredondo-Garcia examined neonatal outcomes of children born to women with tuberculosis. 38. Jana et al. studied perinatal outcomes in pregnancies complicated by pulmonary tuberculosis, providing insights into maternal and neonatal health. 39. Asuquo et al. conducted a case-control study on the risk of adverse perinatal outcomes due to tuberculosis during pregnancy. 40. Jana et al. also investigated obstetrical outcomes among women with extrapulmonary tuberculosis. 41. Kothari, Mahadevan, and Girling analyzed tuberculosis and pregnancy outcomes in a high-prevalence area in London. 42. Heywood et al. surveyed pregnant women with tuberculosis at the Port Moresby General Hospital, documenting their clinical outcomes. 43. Bjerkedal, Bahna, and Lehmann studied the course and outcome of pregnancy in women with pulmonary tuberculosis. 44. Nhan-Chang and Jones reviewed tuberculosis in pregnancy, providing clinical insights into its management. 45. Dara et al. traced the history and evolution of immigration medical screening for tuberculosis, highlighting its public health significance. 46. Cuevas et al. evaluated LED fluorescence microscopy for diagnosing pulmonary tuberculosis in a multi-country cross-sectional study.
